title: 'A Christmas Carol' (In the bleak mid-winter)
short: Written for Scribner's Monthly (January 1872), collected in 1875, and made famous by Holst's tune 'Cranham' (1906) and Harold Darke's anthem (1909).
body: Rossetti wrote the poem in response to a request for a Christmas poem from the American magazine Scribner's Monthly, where it appeared in January 1872; it was collected in Goblin Market, The Prince's Progress, and Other Poems (1875). Gustav Holst's congregational tune 'Cranham' was printed in The English Hymnal (1906), edited by Ralph Vaughan Williams; Harold Darke's more elaborate choral setting dates from 1909. Hymn and anthem versions often omit a stanza or alter words (Darke's anthem, for instance, drops the stanza on the angels and Mary), so the archive text, with five stanzas, is the poet's full poem.

title: An English winter at Bethlehem
short: The Nativity is set in a northern winter of frost and snow, an imaginative transposition rather than a picture of Palestine.
body: The Gospels give no season for Christ's birth, and Bethlehem rarely sees snow; Rossetti deliberately sets the Incarnation in an English mid-winter, so that the cold, hard earth becomes an image of the world into which Christ comes. The personified wind that 'made moan' and the repetitions of 'Snow on snow' create the stillness of the scene. The past tense and 'Long ago' frame it as a story, before the second stanza moves into theological statement.

title: 'hard as iron ... like a stone'
short: The frozen earth and water echo Job 38:30 ('The waters are hid as with a stone') and the curses of iron heaven and earth in Leviticus 26:19 and Deuteronomy 28:23.
body: In Job 38:29-30 God asks Job who has made the frost, when 'The waters are hid as with a stone, and the face of the deep is frozen'. In Leviticus 26:19 the punishment of disobedience is a heaven 'as iron' and an earth 'as brass', and in Deuteronomy 28:23 the terms are reversed: heaven 'brass' and the earth 'iron', which is closest to Rossetti's line. The allusions suggest a fallen, hardened creation awaiting redemption, a reading strengthened when the next stanza speaks of heaven and earth fleeing away.

title: Repetition and short lines
short: Repetitions ('snow on snow, / Snow on snow') and dwindling line lengths build the effect of snow settling layer upon layer.
body: Each stanza alternates longer and shorter lines, and the fifth to eighth lines of the first stanza contract from a full line to two words, 'Long ago'. The refrain-like 'In the bleak mid-winter' returns in the second stanza, binding the first two stanzas together. The simplicity of the language is a deliberate choice for a carol, a song for congregations and children.

title: 'Heaven cannot hold Him'
short: Echoes Solomon's prayer that 'heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee' (1 Kings 8:27), setting God's infinity against the small stable.
body: Solomon, dedicating the Temple, admits that no building can contain God, since even 'heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee' (1 Kings 8:27). Rossetti sets this immensity beside the humble sufficiency of 'A stable-place'. The paradox of the infinite God contained in an infant is the central theme of Christian Nativity poetry, from medieval carols to Milton's 'On the Morning of Christ's Nativity'.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, 1 Kings 8:27

anchor: Heaven and earth shall flee away
title: 'Heaven and earth shall flee away'
short: The Second Coming: at Christ's return in glory, the present heaven and earth will pass away (Revelation 20:11; 21:1).
body: The stanza places the first coming (in humility) against the second (in majesty), following Revelation 20:11, where 'the earth and the heaven fled away' before the one on the great white throne, and 21:1, 'a new heaven and a new earth'. Compare Christ's words, 'Heaven and earth shall pass away' (Matthew 24:35). The contrast is a staple of Advent preaching, the season of the two comings that precedes Christmas.

title: The sufficient stable
short: The humble stable is enough for 'The Lord God Almighty', the Incarnation's paradox of greatness in lowliness.
body: Luke 2:7 records the manger 'because there was no room for them in the inn'; tradition supplied the stable. The word 'sufficed', taken up as 'Enough' in the next stanza, becomes the poem's keyword: what is small and poor is enough for God, preparing the final claim that the speaker's poor gift of a heart is enough too. The stanza ends on the full title 'The Lord God Almighty / Jesus Christ', a credal affirmation of Christ's divinity.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Luke 2:7

title: Cherubim and seraphim
short: The highest orders of angels in the traditional hierarchy, whose worship 'night and day' recalls the heavenly creatures who 'rest not day and night' (Revelation 4:8).
body: Cherubim guard Eden and the Ark in the Hebrew Bible; seraphim sing 'Holy, holy, holy' in Isaiah 6:2-3. Christian tradition, systematised by Pseudo-Dionysius, placed seraphim and cherubim at the top of nine angelic orders, with 'Angels and archangels' (st. 4) below. The heavenly worship 'night and day' (Revelation 4:8) contrasts with the earthly sufficiency of milk and hay. The Hebrew plural ending -im is kept.

anchor: The ox and ass and camel
title: The ox, ass and camel
short: The ox and ass come from tradition based on Isaiah 1:3; the camel from the Magi and Isaiah 60:6.
body: No animals are named in the Gospels' Nativity, but the ox and ass entered tradition from Isaiah 1:3 ('The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib'), read by early Christian writers as prophecy, and they appear in medieval Nativity art. The camel belongs to the Magi, whose gifts were linked with Isaiah 60:6 ('The multitude of camels ... they shall bring gold and incense'). Rossetti lets the beasts' simple adoration be 'Enough', like the milk and hay.

title: Mary's kiss
short: Where angels may have thronged the air, only Mary worships with a kiss, the intimate love that surpasses heavenly praise.
body: The fourth stanza is hedged ('May have gathered there') because the angels' presence at the manger is not recorded in Luke, where angels appear to the shepherds. The certain thing is Mary's human, bodily tenderness: 'In her maiden bliss' affirms her virginity, and 'the Beloved' borrows the language of the Song of Songs, read allegorically as the love between God and the soul. Darke's anthem omits this stanza, but in the full poem it prepares the speaker's own offering of love.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Song of Solomon 2:16

title: The shepherd and the wise man
short: The speaker imagines the gifts of Luke's shepherds and Matthew's Magi, but has neither lamb nor treasure.
body: The shepherds come from Luke 2:8-20, the wise men (Magi) from Matthew 2:1-11, who bring gold, frankincense and myrrh. A shepherd's lamb also anticipates Christ as the 'Lamb of God' (John 1:29). The conditional 'If I were' acknowledges the speaker's poverty and distance in time, and the dash after 'do my part' marks the pause before the answer. The two figures represent the poor and the learned, so that the speaker, who is neither, stands for every worshipper.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Luke 2:8

The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, John 1:29

title: 'Give my heart'
short: The poem ends with the gift anyone can give, the heart, echoing Proverbs 23:26: 'My son, give me thine heart.'
body: The final stanza turns from narrative to the first person, the move that has made the poem a congregational hymn. The offering of the heart answers the stanza's question 'What can I give Him, / Poor as I am?' and fulfils the poem's logic of sufficiency: as the stable and the manger were enough, so is a poor person's love. The biblical source is Proverbs 23:26, and the idea that God desires the heart rather than sacrifice runs through the Psalms (Psalm 51:16-17).
